open_questions: Exact enrolled text of SB 280's grandfathering/carve-out for pre-2016 county ordinances (reported during floor debate as benefiting Flagler County; a Broward County claim was disputed on the floor by Sen. Pizzo, who said Broward has no such ordinance). Direct fetch of the enrolled text and bill-analysis pages from flsenate.gov timed out twice in this session — needs direct confirmation.
Whether any successor vacation-rental preemption bill was filed or enacted in the 2025 Florida session (not researched here); assume current law is the 2014 version of s. 509.032(7) until verified.

Several third-party host guides still describe SB 280 as enacted/effective July 1, 2024 (written pre-veto). Any downstream content must not rely on them; the flsenate.gov bill record (veto message transmitted) is controlling.

DBPR publishes no FAQ on the state-vs-local division of vacation-rental authority after the veto; if the SmartPR product presents operator guidance, the only official posture available is the AG opinion interpreting s. 509.032(7) plus the division's licensing guide.

requirements.agency: Florida Legislature / Office of the Governor
requirements.applies_when: Applies to anyone relying on 2024-era summaries of SB 280: the bill's preemption framework, local-registration rules, and advertising-platform rules have NO legal force because the bill did not become law.
requirements.citation: flsenate.gov bill record for SB 280 (2024), 'Last Action: Veto Message transmitted to Secretary of State'
requirements.notes: CRITICAL: much third-party coverage (e.g., a widely circulated host guide claiming SB 280 was 'in full effect on July 1, 2024') was written before the June 27, 2024 veto and is wrong. The veto letter states the bill would have prevented local governments from enforcing existing ordinances or passing new local measures exclusively applying to vacation rentals, with any such measure required to apply to all residential properties. Current law therefore remains the 2014 version of s. 509.032(7), F.S.
requirements.timeline: Vetoed June 27, 2024 (veto message transmitted to Secretary of State, per Senate bill record). It had passed the Senate 23-16 and the House 60-51 in March 2024.
requirements.title: SB 280 (2024) was vetoed and never became law

requirements.agency: State of Florida (DBPR, Division of Hotels and Restaurants) vs. local governments
requirements.applies_when: Applies to all Florida local governments regulating public lodging establishments and public food service establishments, including vacation rentals.
requirements.notes: Statutory text: 'The regulation of public lodging establishments and public food service establishments, including, but not limited to, sanitation standards, inspections, training and testing of personnel, and matters related to the nutritional content and marketing of foods offered in such establishments, is preempted to the state.' Carve-out: this does NOT preempt local governments' or local enforcement districts' authority to inspect for compliance with the Florida Building Code and the Florida Fire Prevention Code (ss. 553.80 and 633.206).
requirements.title: State preemption of public lodging/food service regulation (s. 509.032(7)(a))

requirements.applies_when: Applies to any Florida local government considering an ordinance that would ban vacation rentals in a jurisdiction/zone or cap how often or how long they may be rented.
requirements.citation: Fla. Stat. s. 509.032(7)(b), as amended by ch. 2014-71, Laws of Fla.
requirements.notes: Statutory text: 'A local law, ordinance, or regulation may not prohibit vacation rentals or regulate the duration or frequency of rental of vacation rentals.' AG opinions interpret this to mean zoning cannot be used to prohibit vacation rentals in an area where residential use is otherwise allowed. History: the 2011 version also barred restricting use or regulating based solely on classification/use/occupancy; the 2014 amendment narrowed the preemption to the prohibit/duration/frequency formulation above.
requirements.title: Local governments may not prohibit vacation rentals or regulate rental duration/frequency (s. 509.032(7)(b))

requirements.applies_when: Applies to any local vacation-rental law, ordinance, or regulation adopted on or before June 1, 2011 — the preemption in (7)(b) does not apply to it.
requirements.citation: Fla. Stat. s. 509.032(7)(b): 'This paragraph does not apply to any local law, ordinance, or regulation adopted on or before June 1, 2011.'
requirements.notes: This is the only statutory grandfathering clause that survived into current law (SB 280's broader grandfathering died with the veto). Any local ordinance adopted after June 1, 2011 that prohibits vacation rentals or regulates their rental duration/frequency is preempted and unenforceable.
requirements.title: Grandfathering: ordinances adopted on or before June 1, 2011 survive (s. 509.032(7)(b))

requirements.applies_when: Applies only to a local law, ordinance, or regulation exclusively relating to property valuation as a criterion for vacation rental that must be approved by the state land planning agency pursuant to an area of critical state concern designation.
requirements.notes: Narrow carve-out: (7)(b) does not apply to a local law exclusively relating to property valuation as a vacation-rental criterion when approval by the state land planning agency is required under an area-of-critical-state-concern designation.
requirements.title: Property-valuation/area-of-critical-state-concern exception (s. 509.032(7)(c))

requirements.applies_when: Applies to local governments and local enforcement districts inspecting public lodging establishments, including vacation rentals, for compliance with the Florida Building Code and Florida Fire Prevention Code.
requirements.notes: Confirmed in the SB 280-era bill analysis as current law: local governments retain authority to conduct building/fire code inspections of vacation rentals. Local governments may also enforce generally applicable (not vacation-rental-specific) ordinances — e.g., noise, parking, trash — consistent with the AG opinion guidance.
requirements.title: Local building and fire code inspections of vacation rentals remain local (s. 509.032(7)(a) carve-out)

requirements.agency: Florida DBPR, Division of Hotels and Restaurants (state role)
requirements.applies_when: Applies to any person renting an entire vacation rental unit more than three times in a calendar year for periods of less than 30 days or 1 calendar month (whichever is less), or advertising it as regularly rented to guests.
requirements.citation: Fla. Stat. ss. 509.241, 509.242(1)(c); DBPR vacation rental guide

forms.name: Vacation Rental license application (online via DBPR licensing portal)

requirements.notes: DBPR licenses vacation rentals in two classifications: Vacation Rental–Condominium (unit(s) in a condo/coop) and Vacation Rental–Dwelling (single-family/townhouse/duplex-triplex-quadruplex up to 4 units). Operating without a license is a second-degree misdemeanor (s. 509.241(1)). Room-only rentals (not the whole unit) are not public lodging and need no DBPR license but may face local rules.
requirements.title: DBPR state licensing of vacation rentals (ss. 509.241-509.242)

requirements.agency: Local government (proposed framework under vetoed SB 280 — historical reference only)
requirements.applies_when: Would have applied to any local government establishing a vacation rental registration program; it never took effect. Included only so downstream readers know what the vetoed bill would have allowed.
requirements.fees: Enrolled bill allowed a 'reasonable' per-unit processing fee and annual renewal fee plus a reasonable post-registration building/fire-code inspection fee; amounts never defined or enacted.
requirements.notes: The enrolled bill would have limited local registration conditions to exactly 7 items: (1) owner/operator/premises identifying info; (2) proof of division license with unique identifier; (3) all required tax registrations/receipts/certificates (DOR, county, municipality); (4) keep information current; (5) pay in full all recorded municipal/county code liens; (6) designate a 24/7 responsible party able to receive legal notice of violations; (7) state and comply with a maximum overnight occupancy (see FL_DRAFT_SPRE_0009). Locals would have had to accept/deny within 15 business days.
requirements.title: SB 280 (vetoed): proposed closed-list local registration requirements — NOT IN FORCE

requirements.agency: Local government (proposed framework under vetoed SB 280 — historical reference only)
requirements.applies_when: Would have applied to local registration programs under SB 280; never took effect.
requirements.notes: Enrolled text: maximum overnight occupancy not to exceed 'either two persons per bedroom, plus an additional two persons in one common area; or more than two persons per bedroom if there is at least 50 square feet per person, plus an additional two persons in one common area, whichever is greater.' DBPR's own fire-safety rules (Fla. Admin. Code R. 69A-43.018) separately address occupancy limits for transient lodging in one/two-family dwellings — those state rules remain in force.
requirements.title: SB 280 (vetoed): proposed occupancy cap formula — NOT IN FORCE

requirements.agency: Advertising platforms / vacation rental operators (proposed framework under vetoed SB 280 — historical reference only)
requirements.applies_when: Would have applied to platforms advertising Florida vacation rentals; never took effect.
requirements.fees: Division could have fined platforms up to $1,000 per offense (unenacted).
requirements.notes: The bill would have preempted regulation of advertising platforms to the state, required platforms to display the vacation rental license number (+ local registration number if applicable), verify listing validity via a DBPR vacation rental information system (effective Jan 1, 2026), remove listings of suspended/unlicensed rentals within 15 business days of notice, and collect/remit tourist development and sales taxes (ss. 125.0104, 125.0108, 205.044, 212.03, 212.0305, 212.055) on platform-paid transactions. None of this is law.
requirements.title: SB 280 (vetoed): proposed advertising-platform regulation and tax collection — NOT IN FORCE

requirements.agency: Local government (proposed framework under vetoed SB 280 — historical reference only)
requirements.applies_when: Would have applied to local governments enforcing a registration program under SB 280; never took effect.
requirements.notes: Enrolled enforcement framework: fine up to $500 per operator violation of registration requirements (lien/foreclosure permitted if not homestead-protected); suspension up to 30/60/90 days for qualifying violation patterns on the premises (with opportunity to cure non-occupancy violations, 21-day minimum notice before suspension start, appeal to circuit court within 30 days); revocation/refusal to renew only for (a) three prior suspensions, (b) unsatisfied recorded municipal/county lien (60-day cure), or (c) a final court order directing termination of vacation-rental use. A pre-2016 county-ordinance carve-out was reported during floor debate (Flagler County named; a Broward claim was disputed on the floor) — exact enrolled text of this carve-out was not verified; see open questions.
requirements.title: SB 280 (vetoed): local registration enforcement powers — NOT IN FORCE

requirements.agency: Florida DBPR, Division of Hotels and Restaurants
requirements.applies_when: Applies to operators and local governments looking for official DBPR guidance on the state/local division of vacation-rental authority.
requirements.citation: DBPR Guide to Vacation Rentals and Timeshare Projects (myfloridalicense.com)
requirements.notes: The division's public guide addresses definitions, license classifications, and the license application process, but contains no FAQ or guidance on SB 280, preemption, or the state's role vs. the local role post-veto. Tax registrations (sales tax via DOR; tourist development taxes via county) are county/DOR matters, not DBPR. Direct flsenate.gov page fetches for the statute and bill analysis timed out in this session, so statute quotations above were sourced from the AG opinion and bill-analysis search snippets; direct confirmation against Online Sunshine is recommended before quoting.
requirements.title: No DBPR post-SB 280 local-role guidance exists (division guidance covers licensing, not preemption)
